sources.title: Warren Presses Treasury Secretary Bessent and Fed Chair Powell to Rule Out Taxpayer-Funded Bailout for Cryptocurrency Billionaires
sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
sources.access_notes: Primary committee release opened. It says Warren requested written assurance by Feb. 27 and quoted her concern that intervention could enrich Trump family-linked World Liberty Financial.

sources.title: Treasury Secretary Invokes Bitcoin Creator Satoshi Nakamoto in Plea for Clarity Act
sources.access_notes: Article opened. It reports Bessent’s July 30 call for an immediate Senate vote; it does not support the original quoted wording.

supported_facts: On Feb. 19, 2026, Warren asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell for written assurance that their agencies would not use taxpayer funds to bail out crypto billionaires.
Warren argued such intervention could directly enrich Trump and his family’s cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial.
Separately, Decrypt reports Bessent urged an immediate Senate vote on the CLARITY Act on July 30, 2026.
unsupported_original_claims: The entry dates Warren’s bailout letter to the July–August 2026 period; the Senate committee dates it Feb. 19, 2026.
The quoted Bessent line “essential to the future viability of bitcoin and digital asset markets in the U.S.” was not found in the opened source.
The letter says intervention could enrich WLFI; it does not itself establish that the Trump family maintained ownership or received a benefit.

corrected_claim.title: Warren Requests No-Bailout Pledge for Crypto Billionaires
corrected_claim.claim: On Feb. 19, 2026, Senator Elizabeth Warren asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Fed Chair Jerome Powell to rule out taxpayer-funded support for crypto billionaires, arguing that a bailout could enrich Trump family-linked World Liberty Financial.

access_notes: The official Senate committee release and Decrypt report were directly opened. They document separate February and July events; the corrected claim covers only the February letter.
evidence_gap: No source in this packet supports the original timeline or Bessent quote as written. Warren’s letter attributes a possible conflict; it does not prove actual bailout plans or realized enrichment.

sources.title: What We Know So Far About 2026 ACA Marketplace Enrollment, Premiums, and Deductibles
sources.access_notes: KFF analysis opened. Its reported premium and deductible averages and enrollment estimates are explicit; it does not report the entry’s Ohio/Oklahoma percentages or February count.

supported_facts: After enhanced tax credits expired at the end of 2025, average monthly Marketplace premium payments rose 58%, from $113 to $178.
Average Marketplace deductibles rose 37% (about $1,027) to $3,786 in 2026.
KFF estimated effectuated enrollment could fall from 22.3 million in 2025 to about 17.5 million, potentially as low as 16.5 million, in 2026.
unsupported_original_claims: The statement that roughly 3 million fewer people had coverage by February 2026 is not the same measure or timing as KFF’s projected 2026 effectuated-enrollment decline.
The claimed nearly one-third enrollment losses in Ohio and Oklahoma are not supported by this source.
“Strips coverage” assigns a specific causal outcome not demonstrated by these aggregate cost and projected-enrollment measures.

corrected_claim.title: ACA Marketplace Costs Rise as Enrollment Is Projected to Fall
corrected_claim.claim: KFF reported that average monthly net ACA Marketplace premiums rose 58%, from $113 to $178, and average deductibles rose 37% to $3,786 in 2026 after enhanced tax credits expired. KFF projected lower effectuated enrollment; it did not verify the original February or state-specific figures.

access_notes: KFF page was directly opened and read.
evidence_gap: The exact February 2026 coverage comparison and Ohio/Oklahoma one-third losses require a dated state-level enrollment source; KFF’s national projections cannot substitute for those claims.

sources.title: Espionage Act experts warn journalists of looming prosecutions
sources.access_notes: Event report opened. It describes the July 1 discussion and attributes prospective warnings to lawyers Abbe Lowell and Mark Zaid.

supported_facts: At a July 1, 2025 National Press Club event, lawyers Abbe Lowell and Mark Zaid warned that journalists could face Espionage Act prosecutions under the administration.
The event report discusses Attorney General Pam Bondi’s April memo and advises reporters to consider the risks of publishing sensitive leaked material.
unsupported_original_claims: The source does not establish that Trump or senior officials were actively seeking a test case against a reporter.
The private Trump quote “Why not the press?”, the senior official’s alleged text-message statement, and the Iran-leak investigation as a selected vehicle are not corroborated by this event report.

corrected_claim.title: Press-Freedom Lawyers Warn of Possible Espionage Act Prosecutions
corrected_claim.claim: At a July 1, 2025 National Press Club event, attorneys Abbe Lowell and Mark Zaid warned that journalists could face Espionage Act prosecution and discussed the implications of DOJ’s revised leak-investigation policy.

access_notes: National Press Club report directly opened; no source was found in the packet for the attributed private statements or an administration test-case plan.
evidence_gap: The alleged administration effort to select a reporter for an Espionage Act test prosecution needs direct corroboration, such as the original Rolling Stone reporting and its underlying sources.

sources.title: How many children are affected by parental immigrant detention?
sources.access_notes: Brookings page opened. It links to the authors’ data appendix and estimates children affected by parental detention.

sources.title: The administration has detained 400,000 immigrants. What do we know about their children?
sources.access_notes: Companion Brookings analysis cited in the existing packet proposal for detention context.

supported_facts: Brookings estimated about 205,000 children experienced a parent’s immigration detention from Jan. 20, 2025 through Apr. 9, 2026, including roughly 145,000 U.S.-citizen children.
The 205,000 figure is an estimate of children affected by parental detention, not a count of deported parents.
unsupported_original_claims: The title converts detention into 205,000 parental deportations or permanent loss of a parent.
The July 2025 ICE directive details, CNN count of children stranded, and ORR tip/arrest totals are not established by these Brookings sources.

corrected_claim.title: Brookings Estimates 205,000 Children Experienced Parental Immigration Detention
corrected_claim.claim: Brookings estimated that about 205,000 children, including roughly 145,000 U.S.-citizen children, experienced a parent’s immigration detention between Jan. 20, 2025 and Apr. 9, 2026. The figure measures detention exposure, not deportation.

access_notes: The Brookings estimate page was opened; the related article is linked as contextual evidence. The estimate is modeled rather than a direct census.
evidence_gap: Separate primary or high-quality sources are needed for the alleged ICE directive, CNN’s September 2025 count, and ORR-to-ICE tip and sponsor-arrest numbers.

sources.title: U.S. FEC commissioner-chair says Trump removed her from office
sources.access_notes: Reuters report linked in the packet; it covers Weintraub’s contested removal and the four-vote threshold.

sources.title: FEC approves two advisory opinions; elects Commissioner Shana M. Broussard as Chair effective July 1, 2025; Commissioner Allen J. Dickerson announces departure
sources.access_notes: Official FEC release opened. It says Dickerson’s departure took effect immediately and identifies a matter failing to receive four affirmative votes.

sources.title: The FEC has been crippled for more than a year. The 2026 midterms approach.
sources.access_notes: NOTUS report opened. It reports a de facto shutdown after quorum loss and at least 195 pending enforcement matters as of early March, citing FEC Chair Shana Broussard.

sources.title: FEC Shutdown Leaves Cases in Limbo
sources.access_notes: URL in the existing proposal; use for case-backlog reporting, not as primary confirmation of every number in the original.

supported_facts: FEC action requiring a vote needs four affirmative commissioner votes; the agency fell below quorum after commissioner vacancies and departures.
NOTUS reports the commission had at least 195 pending enforcement matters in early March 2026, citing Chair Shana Broussard.
unsupported_original_claims: The “nearly 80%” duration is not established by the directly reviewed FEC release or the cited NOTUS article text.
The description overstates that the agency could take no action of any kind; the documented constraint concerns matters requiring commission votes.
The zero-dollar FY2026 fine claim, February 2026 nominee details, and exact “May 1 formal shutdown” characterization are not verified by the sources reviewed here.

corrected_claim.title: FEC Lacks Voting Quorum as Enforcement Backlog Reaches at Least 195 Matters
corrected_claim.claim: After commissioner vacancies left the FEC without the four votes required for commission action, NOTUS reported at least 195 pending enforcement matters in early March 2026, citing the commission’s chair.

access_notes: Official FEC release and NOTUS report were directly opened; Reuters link and additional NOTUS backlog link were carried over from the prior packet. No percentage-duration claim is retained.
evidence_gap: A dated FEC roster and primary enforcement statistics are needed to quantify the precise no-quorum interval, the 80% calculation, fine assessments, and the exact May 1 start date.

sources.title: EFTA00028716
sources.access_notes: DOJ-hosted PDF triggered an age-verification gate during this check. Its text was cross-checked against the OCR transcription at EpsteinScan; the PDF is a prosecutor email summarizing flight records, not the underlying logs.

sources.title: Attorney General Pamela Bondi Releases First Phase of Declassified Epstein Files
sources.access_notes: Official release establishes the DOJ document collection context, not the details of an individual flight.

sources.title: EFTA00028716.pdf - EpsteinScan
sources.access_notes: Third-party OCR transcription of the DOJ document was readable; used only to verify the email’s text, not to validate the separate raw flight log.

supported_facts: The January 8, 2020 prosecutor email says newly received flight records listed Trump as a passenger on at least eight flights between 1993 and 1996.
The email says some flights included Marla Maples, Tiffany Trump, or Eric Trump.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited DOJ email does not contain the May 15, 1994 itinerary, N988JE aircraft identifier, Reagan National/Teterboro routing, or passenger list naming Mark Middleton and Tiffany’s nanny.
The statement that this is the only flight with infant Tiffany is unsupported by the email.

corrected_claim.title: DOJ Prosecutor Email Says Trump Was Listed on at Least Eight Epstein-Jet Flights
corrected_claim.claim: A January 2020 DOJ prosecutor email summarizing flight records said Donald Trump was listed on at least eight Epstein-aircraft flights from 1993 to 1996 and named family members who traveled on some flights.

access_notes: The official PDF was age-gated by the scraper; its OCR text was read from a third-party archive. The primary email is distinct from the raw flight logs.
evidence_gap: The exact May 15, 1994 manifest and route require the underlying official flight-log page. The third-party itinerary reconstruction is not sufficient to verify every passenger and route detail.

sources.title: U.S. spy agency data on DOGE website was unclassified, but not meant for public release
sources.access_notes: Reuters article opened. It identifies aggregate NRO headcount and total-wage data and quotes the agency spokesperson.

sources.title: Agency data shared on DOGE site sparks concern in intelligence community
sources.access_notes: Source linked by the existing proposal for contextual reporting; Reuters directly confirms the aggregate posting.

supported_facts: DOGE’s website displayed National Reconnaissance Office headcount and total wage data in February 2025.

An NRO spokesperson told Reuters the information was unclassified but not intended for public release and that the agency was working to remedy the posting; Reuters said it remained visible on Feb. 21.
unsupported_original_claims: The reviewed sources do not show DOGE publicly uploading individual employees’ home addresses, salaries, or performance reviews.
The “tens of thousands” exposed, union lawsuits over that posting, court takedown orders, and continuing public availability are not established by the NRO aggregate-data report.

corrected_claim.title: DOGE Website Posted NRO Headcount and Wage Data Not Intended for Public Release
corrected_claim.claim: Reuters reported that DOGE’s website displayed aggregate National Reconnaissance Office headcount and total-wage data in February 2025. The NRO said the data was unclassified but not intended for public release and was still online on Feb. 21.

access_notes: Reuters story directly opened and read. It concerns aggregate agency data, not a personnel-file breach or individual records.
evidence_gap: A separate credible source is needed to establish any public release of individually identifiable federal-worker data, the number of people affected, related litigation, or court orders.

sources.title: Social Security Announces Workforce and Organization Plans
sources.access_notes: Official SSA release opened. It states the target and describes voluntary departures, retirement incentives, and possible future reduction-in-force actions.

supported_facts: SSA announced a target of 50,000 employees, down from approximately 57,000, on Feb. 28, 2025.
The agency said much of the reduction was expected through retirement, voluntary separation, and resignation; additional RIF actions were possible, but no RIF start date had been set.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited release does not support a July 2025 DOGE mandate to terminate thousands of employees.
The claims that standard civil-service protections were bypassed, essential operations were disrupted, or the cuts were intended to break SSA are not established by this release.

corrected_claim.title: SSA Sets Workforce Target of 50,000, Down From About 57,000
corrected_claim.claim: On Feb. 28, 2025, SSA announced a target to reduce staffing from about 57,000 to 50,000, expecting many departures through voluntary programs and retirement while retaining the possibility of later RIF actions.

access_notes: SSA’s primary press release was directly opened and read.
evidence_gap: The July date, number of involuntary terminations, civil-service process, and operational effects require dated SSA or OPM records and independent reporting.

sources.title: Reversal at U.S. Justice Department says media records can be seized in leak probes
sources.access_notes: Reuters article opened. It reports Bondi’s April 25 memo reversing Biden-era restrictions and lowering the bar for subpoenas and other process in leak investigations.

sources.title: Justice Manual § 9-13.000 Obtaining Evidence
sources.access_notes: Official DOJ manual linked in the packet for the policy framework; it does not document an August subpoena campaign.

supported_facts: On April 25, 2025, Bondi issued a memo reversing Biden-era limits on prosecutors’ use of subpoenas, court orders, and search warrants for media records and testimony in leak investigations.
Reuters reported that procedural safeguards remained in the revised policy.
unsupported_original_claims: No source reviewed supports the alleged August 2025 sweeping subpoenas after journalists’ arrests or a demand that reporters disclose confidential sources in a coordinated campaign.
The claimed intent to terrorize whistleblowers and demonstrated chilling effect are not established by the cited policy change.

corrected_claim.title: Bondi DOJ Reverses Restrictions on Media-Record Process in Leak Investigations
corrected_claim.claim: On April 25, 2025, the Justice Department reversed Biden-era restrictions and made it easier for prosecutors to seek journalists’ records and testimony in leak investigations, while retaining procedural safeguards.

access_notes: Reuters report was directly opened; the DOJ manual is the official procedural reference. The policy event occurred in April, not August.
evidence_gap: A dated court filing, subpoena, or credible report is needed to substantiate the claimed August arrests and broad effort to compel confidential sources.

sources.title: McMaster out and turnover on the White House “A Team” continues at a steady clip
sources.access_notes: Brookings article opened. It states first-year A-Team turnover was 34% and turnover had reached 48% just over 14 months into the administration.

sources.title: President Trump and the “shallow state”
sources.access_notes: Brookings source linked in the input; relevant to later turnover context and counts of senior positions.

supported_facts: Brookings reported first-year turnover of 34% among Trump White House senior “A-Team” positions, compared with 17% for Reagan and 9% for Obama.
By just over 14 months, Brookings reported 48% turnover in those positions.
Brookings’ broader turnover accounting lists four Trump chiefs of staff in the first term, not six.
unsupported_original_claims: The 65% rate is not a year-one figure in the opened Brookings article; the 34% first-year and 48% at 14 months measures are explicit.
The seven listed officials are not six chiefs of staff; most held other positions.
The claim that six chiefs served across Trump’s presidency is not supported by the Brookings count reviewed.

corrected_claim.title: Brookings Reports 34% First-Year Turnover on Trump’s White House A-Team
corrected_claim.claim: Brookings calculated 34% turnover among Trump White House senior A-Team positions in his first year, rising to 48% just over 14 months into his presidency. Its separate accounting lists four chiefs of staff during the first term.

access_notes: Both Brookings links were opened or cross-checked; the first directly provides the year-one and 14-month percentages.
evidence_gap: The original’s list of seven departures should not be presented as chiefs of staff; each named person’s office and departure date needs separate sourcing if retained.
